software-engineer.title: Software Engineer
software-engineer.tagline: Your path from zero → job ready.

tracks.title: Programming
tracks.what: The core skill everything else builds on — variables, control flow, functions, and at least one language you know deeply.
tracks.why: Every other skill in this roadmap assumes you can already write and reason about code.
learn: Pick one language and go deep (Python, Java, or C++)

tracks.title: Git
tracks.what: Version control — tracking changes, branching, and collaborating without overwriting each other's work.
tracks.why: Every real engineering team uses it; not knowing Git is an instant red flag in interviews.

tracks.title: Data Structures
tracks.what: Arrays, hash maps, trees, graphs, and the algorithms that operate on them.
tracks.why: This is what most technical interviews actually test — not because you'll invert a binary tree at work, but because it signals how you reason about problems.

chain.title: APIs
chain.what: How software components talk to each other over a network — usually REST or GraphQL.
chain.why: Almost every real application is built from services talking through APIs.

chain.title: Databases
chain.what: Where an application's data actually lives — relational (SQL) or non-relational (NoSQL).
chain.why: Every non-trivial application needs to store and query data reliably.

chain.title: Testing
chain.what: Writing code that verifies your other code actually works.
chain.why: The difference between "it works on my machine" and something a team can trust in production.

chain.title: System Design
chain.what: How to structure a larger application — services, scaling, trade-offs.
chain.why: Senior interviews and real architecture decisions both live here.

chain.title: Projects
chain.what: Build something real, end to end.
chain.why: This is what actually gets noticed on a CV — a working project beats a list of completed tutorials.
chain.build: A small full-stack application — a front end, an API, and a real database.

devops.title: DevOps Engineer
devops.tagline: Your path from zero → job ready.

tracks.title: Linux
tracks.what: The operating system layer everything else runs on.
tracks.why: Shell comfort, file permissions, and process management are assumed in every task ahead.

tracks.title: Git
tracks.what: Version control for infrastructure and application code alike.
tracks.why: Every DevOps workflow assumes fluent Git — branching, merging, and history.

tracks.title: Networking
tracks.what: How machines actually talk to each other.
tracks.why: Makes "why is this unreachable" answerable instead of a guessing game.

chain.title: Docker
chain.what: Package an application and its dependencies into a portable container.
chain.why: The unit almost everything downstream (Cloud, CI/CD, Kubernetes) is built around.
chain.build: Containerize a small web application end to end.

chain.title: Cloud
chain.what: AWS, Azure, or GCP — infrastructure you rent instead of own.
chain.why: Pick one and go deep before spreading across all three. The concepts transfer; the exact APIs don't.

chain.title: CI / CD
chain.what: Automate build, test, and deploy.
chain.why: Shipping becomes a routine event, not a stressful manual ritual.

chain.title: Terraform
chain.what: Define infrastructure as code instead of clicking through a cloud console.
chain.why: Reproducible, reviewable, versioned infrastructure — not tribal knowledge.

chain.title: Kubernetes
chain.what: Orchestrate containers at scale.
chain.why: For when a single Docker host isn't enough anymore.

chain.title: Projects
chain.what: Build something real, end to end.
chain.why: This is what actually gets noticed on a CV — not another tutorial completion.
chain.build: A CI/CD pipeline for a real app, or a Terraform-provisioned cluster.

embedded.title: Embedded Engineer
embedded.tagline: Your path from zero → job ready.

tracks.title: C/C++
tracks.what: The languages embedded systems are almost universally written in — direct memory control, no safety net.
tracks.why: Higher-level languages rarely run on the resource-constrained hardware embedded engineers target.

tracks.title: MCU
tracks.what: The actual chip your code runs on — registers, peripherals, interrupts.
tracks.why: Embedded work means thinking in terms of real hardware, not an abstract runtime.

tracks.title: Git
tracks.what: Version control — tracking changes, branching, and collaborating without overwriting each other's work.
tracks.why: Firmware teams use Git just like software teams do — it's not optional.

chain.title: RTOS
chain.what: A real-time operating system — scheduling multiple tasks on constrained hardware with timing guarantees.
chain.why: Most non-trivial embedded systems need more than a single bare-metal loop.

chain.title: CAN
chain.what: Controller Area Network — the bus protocol most automotive and industrial ECUs use to talk to each other.
chain.why: If you're targeting automotive embedded work specifically, CAN fluency is close to mandatory.

chain.title: AUTOSAR
chain.what: A standardized software architecture used across the automotive industry for ECU software.
chain.why: Most automotive OEMs and suppliers build on AUTOSAR — it's a real, specific hiring filter in that industry.

chain.title: Debugging
chain.what: Finding out why embedded code is misbehaving, with far fewer tools than a normal application has.
chain.why: No print statements to spare, sometimes no debugger at all — this is its own skill.
learn: Reading a stack trace on constrained hardware

chain.title: Testing
chain.what: Verifying embedded software actually works — often on real hardware, not just in simulation.
chain.why: A bug in embedded software can mean a real physical failure, not just a crashed app.

chain.title: Projects
chain.what: Build something real, end to end.
chain.why: This is what actually gets noticed on a CV — a working project beats a list of completed tutorials.
chain.build: A small embedded project end to end — reading a sensor, driving an actuator, or a mini CAN-based system.

ai-ml.title: AI / ML Engineer
ai-ml.tagline: Your path from zero → job ready.

tracks.title: Python
tracks.what: The dominant language for ML — readable, with the richest ecosystem of ML libraries.
tracks.why: Nearly every ML framework, tutorial, and job posting assumes Python fluency.

tracks.title: Math for ML
tracks.what: Linear algebra, probability, and calculus — the actual mechanics behind ML algorithms.
tracks.why: Without this, ML stays a black box you can't debug or improve.

tracks.title: Git
tracks.what: Version control — tracking changes, branching, and collaborating without overwriting each other's work.
tracks.why: ML projects still live in real codebases, tracked like any other software.

chain.title: NumPy & Pandas
chain.what: The core Python libraries for numerical computing and tabular data.
chain.why: Almost every ML pipeline starts with cleaning and shaping data in these two libraries.

chain.title: Machine Learning
chain.what: Classical ML — regression, classification, clustering, and the algorithms behind them.
chain.why: Not every problem needs deep learning; this is the foundation before it.

chain.title: Deep Learning
chain.what: Neural networks — the approach behind most modern breakthroughs in vision, language, and beyond.
chain.why: This is where most current ML job postings and research actually live.

chain.title: PyTorch
chain.what: The most widely used deep learning framework in both research and industry.
chain.why: Fluency here is close to a baseline expectation on ML job postings.

chain.title: MLOps
chain.what: Getting a model from a notebook into something that actually runs reliably in production.
chain.why: A model that only works in your notebook isn't a product — this is the gap most ML tutorials skip.

chain.title: Projects
chain.what: Build something real, end to end.
chain.why: This is what actually gets noticed on a CV — a working project beats a list of completed tutorials.
chain.build: An end-to-end ML project — real data, a trained model, actually serving predictions somewhere.

cloud.title: Cloud Engineer
cloud.tagline: Your path from zero → job ready.

tracks.title: Linux
tracks.what: The operating system layer almost all cloud infrastructure runs on.
tracks.why: Shell comfort, file permissions, and process management are assumed in every task ahead.

tracks.title: Networking
tracks.what: How machines actually talk to each other, at cloud scale.
tracks.why: Cloud environments are network-first — VPCs, subnets, and routing are daily concerns.

tracks.title: Git
tracks.what: Version control for infrastructure and application code alike.
tracks.why: Infrastructure-as-code workflows live in Git, reviewed like any other change.

chain.title: Cloud Fundamentals
chain.what: The core services any cloud provider (AWS, Azure, GCP) offers — compute, storage, identity.
chain.why: Pick one provider and go deep; the concepts transfer even though the exact APIs don't.

chain.title: Containers
chain.what: Packaging an application so it runs the same way anywhere — the standard unit cloud infrastructure is built around.
chain.why: Nearly all modern cloud deployments are container-based in some form.

chain.title: Security
chain.what: Identity, access control, and network security in a cloud environment.
chain.why: A misconfigured cloud environment is one of the most common real-world security failures — not optional knowledge.

chain.title: IaC
chain.what: Defining cloud infrastructure as code instead of clicking through a console.
chain.why: Reproducible, reviewable, versioned infrastructure — the standard practice at any real scale.

chain.title: Projects
chain.what: Build something real, end to end.
chain.why: This is what actually gets noticed on a CV — a working project beats a list of completed tutorials.
chain.build: Provision real cloud infrastructure for a small project using IaC, not the console.
